title: A Ledger for the Compass
premise: In the winter of a collapsing republic, Rosalind Brightwater carries coded dispatches into the port town of Vellamere, where the last loyalist garrison waits for a ship that may never come. When the victorious army requisitions the town and seizes the customs ledger containing every name the republic ever trusted, Rosalind must decide whether seven years of careful silence were survival or complicity. Working through the frozen nights with a disgraced archivist and a widow who remembers too much, he reconstructs the true record from memory, fragments, and confession. He gets the truth aboard the morning tide in a copy hidden in plain sight, but chooses to stay behind and sign his own name to it, trading escape for testimony.
about_author: Dominic Delacroix is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing seized records from collapsed governments. He writes historical fiction about the people history forgets to interrogate.

chapters.title: The Weight of Blank Paper
chapters.summary: Rosalind arrives in Vellamere posing as a shipping clerk, carrying coded dispatches sewn into his coat lining. Through his POV we learn the rules of his invisibility: never write, never linger, never be remembered. The beat is wary competence shadowed by exhaustion—he has been invisible so long he barely exists to himself.

chapters.title: A Town That Counts Everything
chapters.summary: Rosalind delivers his dispatches to Colonel Ashe, commander of the doomed garrison, and encounters the customs house ledger: every resident's name, allegiance, and debt recorded by clerk Odile Ferrant. Her POV reveals she keeps the ledger out of stubborn faith that records protect people. The emotional beat is ironic hope neither character trusts.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Silences
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter in Rosalind's POV: the mission seven years ago where his silence saved a family but condemned a courier named Ives, whose fate haunts him. He recites the silences like a catechism. The beat is guilt dressed as discipline, establishing what staying invisible has cost him.

chapters.title: Gunpowder on the Tide
chapters.summary: News arrives that the republican fleet was destroyed; the ship promised to evacuate the garrison will be the last one ever. Odile's POV shows the town pivoting from loyalty to self-preservation, neighbors testing each other with careless questions. The beat is dread spreading like damp through walls.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: The victors' army enters without a battle; Captain Verel requisitions the town and orders all records surrendered, including the customs ledger. Rosalind watches from a warehouse loft as soldiers carry out the book containing every name he was sent to protect. His POV; the beat is horror at how completely identity can be confiscated.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Knows
chapters.summary: Odile, dismissed but not arrested, comes to Rosalind because she saw him memorizing pages weeks earlier. She proposes rebuilding the record from memory before the victors' historians formalize their version. His POV; the beat is terror at being asked to become visible, warring with the pull of Ives's ghost.

chapters.title: The Historian's Method
chapters.summary: Rosalind infiltrates the requisitioned customs house under a labor summons and observes historian Maître Corvain at work—crossing out names, annotating 'disloyal,' building an official past. Corvain's POV briefly humanizes him as a man who believes order requires a single story. The beat is chilling professionalism.

chapters.title: The Widow's Testimony
chapters.summary: Rosalind and Odile seek Marta Quillon, a widow whose husband's name the ledger lists among collaborators though he died resisting. Her POV delivers raw grief and the first recovered truth. The beat is the discovery that memory survives in the people the paper forgot.

chapters.title: Rules of Copying
chapters.summary: Working nights in the chapel vestry, the three establish methods: no ink that smears, no page kept twice, memory checked against memory. Rosalind's POV details the craft of reconstruction while his hands shake. The beat is fragile purpose—the first time in seven years he writes anything down.

chapters.title: Colonel Ashe's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ashe, drinking in the empty garrison, offers Rosalind passage on the evacuation ship if he abandons the project; the colonel believes names are ballast that sinks survivors. Rosalind's POV. The beat is temptation offered kindly, which is harder to refuse than threat.

chapters.title: Ives, Recovered
chapters.summary: Odile finds a fragment proving Ives survived capture and gave up nothing before dying—Rosalind's silence did not buy what he thought it bought. His POV breaks open; he confesses his role to Odile. The beat is grief finally spoken aloud, converting guilt into resolve.

chapters.title: The First Name Erased
chapters.summary: Corvain publishes the provisional register; Marta's husband is officially branded a traitor, and her son is denied work rations. Marta's POV shows consequences arriving fast. The beat is fury and urgency—the record race now has a body count.

chapters.title: A Search of the Vestry
chapters.summary: Soldiers raid the chapel on an informer's tip; Rosalind burns the working copies while Odile stalls the sergeant with bureaucratic theater. His POV, nearly caught, saved by a soldier who once appears in the ledger as a debtor Rosalind once protected. The beat is luck revealing that small mercies compound.

chapters.title: The Informer
chapters.summary: They identify the informer: young Tobias Renk, who traded names for his mother's medicine. Rosalind confronts him and, instead of exposing him, recruits him—Tobias knows which rooms the army searches first. Tobias's POV; the beat is mercy as strategy, and Rosalind choosing differently than his old catechism allows.

chapters.title: Corvain's Doubt
chapters.summary: Corvain discovers an inconsistency between two testimonies he recorded and begins quietly verifying against parish books, brushing against the same truths Rosalind is recovering. Corvain's POV. The beat is the official story cracking from inside its own author.

chapters.title: The Ship Announced
chapters.summary: Proclamation: the evacuation ship sails on the morning tide in four days; those on the approved list only. Ashe gives Rosalind his papers. Rosalind's POV calculates what can be finished in four nights. The beat is a clock starting, tension tightening around every remaining name.

chapters.title: Four Nights
chapters.summary: Montage of the final reconstruction: Marta dictating, Tobias running messages, Odile reconciling figures, Rosalind writing until his fingers bleed, then copying everything onto oiled silk that can be sewn into sailcloth. His POV. The beat is exhausted communion—strangers bound into a single act of witness.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Customs House
chapters.summary: Tobias is caught returning for his mother; under threat he breaks and reveals the vestry. Soldiers seize Odile and the silk copy's hiding place is compromised—but Tobias had already moved it, lying about where. Tobias's POV, anguished. The beat is betrayal and redemption in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Trial of Odile Ferrant
chapters.summary: Corvain presides over Odile's hearing for falsifying records; she answers every question with the true names, forcing them onto the official transcript. Rosalind watches from the gallery, realizing her testimony is itself a record. Her POV. The beat is courage as a form of authorship.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Quay
chapters.summary: Dawn. Rosalind holds boarding papers and the silk copy; the sailcloth of the ship itself is the safest hiding place, but sewing it aboard means going with it. He realizes a record smuggled away changes nothing here—only a signed, public deposition does. His POV. The beat is the climax of decision: escape or testimony.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Rosalind walks into Corvain's office and dictates a full sworn deposition, signing his real name, daring the historian to refute a man standing in front of him; Corvain, privately doubting, files it rather than destroy it. The silk copy sails hidden in the rigging. Rosalind's POV. The beat is triumph purchased with surrender.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Rosalind is detained but not executed—too visible now to disappear quietly—and the epilogue-narration reveals the silk copy surfacing years later, vindicating the town's names, while Odile, released, opens a new ledger with his name first. Final beat: invisibility was never safety; being remembered rightly is the only shelter.
